title: Enhancing Detection of Human Trafficking Act
official_title: To direct the Secretary of Labor to train certain employees of Department of Labor how to effectively detect and assist law enforcement in preventing human trafficking during the course of their official duties, and for other purposes.
likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. Walberg (R-MI) with Rep. McBath (D-GA) and 3 cosponsors; passed the House. A bipartisan, low-cost training mandate on human-trafficking detection has a reasonable path through the Senate, though it has not yet received a vote there.
summary: Directs the Labor Department to train relevant employees to spot human trafficking during their work and refer cases to law enforcement, and to report yearly to Congress.
brief: Directs the Secretary of Labor to train relevant employees to detect human trafficking and refer cases, with annual reports to Congress.

items.main: Names the Act the “Enhancing Detection of Human Trafficking Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

items.main: Defines “human trafficking” for the Act by reference to paragraph (11) of section 103 of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000 (22 U.S.C. 7102).
items.detail: Definitions apply throughout; the term adopts the existing statutory definition rather than creating a new one.

sections.label: Section 3 — Training for Department Personnel to Identify Human Trafficking

items.main: Directs the Secretary of Labor to train relevant employees to detect human trafficking and refer cases.
items.detail: Within 180 days of enactment, the Secretary of Labor must implement training and periodic continuing education for Department of Labor employees whose official duties warrant it. For Wage and Hour Division staff, the Secretary must consider employees in states with a significant increase in oppressive child labor (as defined in the Fair Labor Standards Act). Training covers detecting trafficking, identifying suspected victims and traffickers, and a clear path for referring cases to the Department of Justice and other authorities while protecting victims' rights. 'Human trafficking' is defined by reference to the Trafficking Victims Protection Act of 2000 (22 U.S.C. 7102).

items.main: Requires annual reports to Congress on the training and trafficking referrals.
items.detail: Within one year of first implementing the program and annually after, the Secretary must report to the House Education and Workforce Committee and the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the training provided (including its effectiveness and the number of employees trained) and the number of trafficking-detection cases referred to the Department of Justice and other authorities.

gaps: The bill mandates trafficking-detection training but provides no dedicated funding for the program.
It requires referral of suspected cases to the Department of Justice but does not address what happens to workers identified as potential victims.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Moylan
featured_quotes.text: I am very happy and pleased to be a cosponsor of this measure. As we know, human trafficking is modern-day slavery, Mr. Speaker, and traffickers abuse and exploit millions of victims, especially children, girls, and women, all for commercial gain. This is a serious problem around the globe, Mr. Speaker, and even here at home. We must do more to raise awareness of this crime. The U.S. Department of Labor is on the front lines of detecting human trafficking.
